title: Deeds, Recording, Priorities & Title Problems
originality: All items original to LicensePath. Modeled on the DRE exam blueprint and style only; no actual exam items reproduced.

questions.stem: The chain of title is best described as:
options: The current owner's mailing address history
The sequential recorded history of ownership and encumbrances affecting a parcel
A list of past real estate agents
The property's tax assessment history only
rationales: Mailing address history is unrelated.
Correct. It traces recorded documents affecting the parcel from the earliest record forward.
Agent history is unrelated to chain of title.
Tax assessment is a separate record.

questions.stem: Record title, marketable title, and insurable title differ because:
options: They are three names for the same thing
Record title is what the public record shows, which may not reflect true ownership
Insurable title always equals marketable title
Marketable title is decided only by the assessor
rationales: They are distinct concepts.
Correct. Record title reflects the public record, which can include invalid instruments like forgeries.
A title company can insure over exceptions a buyer might still reasonably object to.
The assessor does not determine marketability.

questions.stem: Marketable title is best described as:
options: Perfect title with zero exceptions
Title reasonably free from doubt that a prudent buyer would accept
Title with an ALTA policy only
Title that has never been sold before
rationales: Perfection is not the standard.
Correct. Marketable title is reasonably free from doubt.
Policy type does not define marketability.
Prior sales history is unrelated.

questions.stem: A preliminary title report is best understood as:
options: A finalized title insurance policy
A guarantee of clear title
An offer to insure on stated terms
A recorded deed
rationales: It is not a finalized policy.
It is not a guarantee.
Correct. It states the conditions under which the company will insure.
It is not itself a deed.

questions.stem: The best practice for reviewing a preliminary report's specific exceptions is to:
options: Wait until the week of closing
Read them on day one of escrow
Let escrow read them silently
Only read them if the buyer asks
rationales: Waiting compresses the time available to clear problems.
Correct. Early review leaves time for curative work.
Agents should personally review, not delegate blindly.
Review should happen regardless of whether asked.

questions.stem: A prelim lists a judgment lien against a name matching the seller's but with a different middle initial and no matching prior address. This is most likely:
options: A confirmed lien against the seller
A wild document requiring an affidavit of identity to clear
Proof the seller has bad credit
Irrelevant and safely ignored
rationales: The mismatched details suggest it may not belong to the seller.
Correct. This is a classic wild document, typically cleared with an affidavit of identity/non-identity.
Credit history is a different matter entirely.
It should not be ignored; it must be reviewed and cleared.

questions.stem: A CLTA policy compared to an ALTA policy typically:
options: Provides broader coverage at a higher premium
Provides narrower, standard coverage at a lower premium
Is required by all lenders
Only applies to commercial property
rationales: That describes ALTA relative to CLTA.
Correct. CLTA is the more limited, standard-coverage baseline, commonly used for owner's policies.
Lenders typically require ALTA-type coverage.
CLTA is common in residential transactions.

questions.stem: ALTA coverage is often required by:
options: Buyers only, never lenders
Lenders, and available as extended owner's coverage
The county recorder
The listing agent
rationales: Lenders commonly require it, not just buyers.
Correct. ALTA is often lender-required and available as enhanced owner's coverage.
The recorder does not require policy type.
Agents do not require policy type.

questions.stem: A forged deed in the chain of title is:
options: Voidable by the innocent purchaser
Void, conveying nothing even to a later good-faith purchaser
Valid once recorded
Cured automatically after ten years
rationales: It is void, not merely voidable.
Correct. A forged deed conveys nothing, regardless of subsequent good-faith reliance.
Recording does not validate a forged instrument.
There is no automatic ten-year cure described here.

questions.stem: Because a forged deed conveys nothing, the practical protection for later innocent purchasers most often comes from:
options: The forger's future cooperation
Title insurance absorbing the loss subject to policy terms
Automatic government compensation
The county recorder's guarantee
rationales: The forger is unlikely to cooperate.
Correct. Title insurance is priced to absorb exactly this kind of catastrophic, low-frequency risk.
No such automatic government compensation exists here.
The recorder does not guarantee title validity.

questions.stem: An unreleased lien from a mortgage that was actually paid off years ago is an example of:
options: A properly cleared title
A title defect requiring a recorded satisfaction or reconveyance
A boundary dispute
A quiet title judgment
rationales: It is not properly cleared until released of record.
Correct. The paid lien remains a visible defect until its satisfaction or reconveyance is recorded.
This is not a boundary issue.
No judgment has occurred yet.

questions.stem: An undisclosed heir surfacing years after an improperly probated estate can:
options: Never affect a later buyer's title
Cloud title even after multiple subsequent sales
Only affect the original decedent's spouse
Be ignored if the property has changed hands
rationales: It can affect later title.
Correct. An omitted heir's interest can surface and cloud title well after subsequent transfers.
It can affect any heir, not only a spouse.
Subsequent sales do not erase the underlying defect.

options: An administrative form filed with the title company
A lawsuit asking a court to determine true ownership
A type of deed
A recording fee waiver
rationales: It is a judicial action, not an administrative form.
Correct. It is a lawsuit resolving disputed or clouded ownership.
It is not a deed type.
It is unrelated to recording fees.

questions.stem: A quiet title action is typically appropriate when:
options: A defect can be cleared with a simple affidavit
A defect cannot be cleared administratively, such as an heir who will not sign a release
The buyer wants a faster closing
The seller wants a lower price
rationales: Simple defects are usually cleared administratively, not through litigation.
Correct. Quiet title is reserved for defects that cannot be resolved without a court.
Quiet title actions take months and slow closings, not speed them.
Price preference is unrelated.

questions.stem: When an agent identifies an unexpected exception on a preliminary report, the correct first step is to:
options: Wait to see if it resolves itself
Route it to the title company's curative department and escrow immediately
Advise the client on the legal remedy personally
Remove it from the file
rationales: Waiting wastes valuable curative time.
Correct. Prompt routing to the professionals who can clear it protects the timeline.
Giving legal advice on remedies exceeds license scope.
Ignoring or removing it from the file does not resolve the defect.

questions.stem: General/standard exceptions in a preliminary report typically include matters that:
options: Are unique to one specific property only
An accurate survey would reveal, or rights of parties in possession
Only apply to commercial property
Never appear in residential transactions
rationales: Specific exceptions, not general ones, are unique to the property.
Correct. Standard exceptions commonly include survey-related and possession-related matters.
They are not limited to commercial property.
They routinely appear in residential preliminary reports.

questions.stem: Title insurance is unusual compared to most insurance because:
options: It insures against future events only
It is priced around a one-time premium protecting against past, existing defects
It requires monthly premiums
It only covers lenders, never owners
rationales: It primarily protects against defects that already exist in the historical record.
Correct. A one-time premium covers risk arising from the property's past.
Title insurance is typically a one-time premium, not a recurring monthly payment.
Owner's policies exist alongside lender's policies.

questions.stem: If a preliminary report reveals a serious defect such as a suspected forged instrument in the chain, the licensee should:
options: Resolve it personally to keep the deal moving
Tell the client the closing date is realistically at risk and an attorney may be needed
Hide the issue from the client until it worsens
Recommend the buyer waive title review
rationales: Resolving serious title defects is outside license scope.
Correct. The client needs an honest timeline assessment and, likely, legal involvement.
Concealing a known issue breaches disclosure obligations.
Waiving title review on a serious defect would be poor advice.
